title: Atomic-Scale Spacing between Copper Facets for the Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide
abstract: DOI: 10.1002/aenm.201903423 a liquid fuel through oligomerization,[6] and ethanol that can be used as a fuel directly or converted to olefins and other fuels. By contrast, methane is not a desirable product since it cannot be converted easily to liquid fuels. Therefore, realizing a catalyst for producing ethylene and ethanol with high selectivity is an attractive objective. Experimental[7,8] and theoretical[9–11] studies have shown that Cu is the only metal capable of forming such products with significant Faradaic efficiency (FE). Extensive investigations of the factors affecting the activity and selectivity of Cu have been carried out,[12] and these efforts have shown that the structure of exposed surface facets,[7–11,13–15] the presence of oxygen vacancies,[16] the oxidation states of Cu,[17–20] the presence of subsurface oxygen,[21–23] the occurrence of grain boundaries,[7,24–26] the surface roughness,[27] the cathode pH,[28,29] and the electric field in the double layer[30,31] influence the activity and selectivity of Cu. Notably, though, the role of atomic-scale spacings between the facets of Cu nanoparticles has not been explored. Moreover, our efforts to explore the role of atomic-scale gaps between Cu surfaces on the activity and selectivity of Cu for the CO2RR were motivated by two theoretical recent reports. The first one based on DFT calculations Copper (Cu) offers a means for producing value-added fuels through the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2), i.e., the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), but designing Cu catalysts with significant Faradaic efficiency to C2+ products remains as a great challenge. This work demonstrates that the high activity and selectivity of Cu to C2+ products can be achieved by atomicscale spacings between two facets of Cu particles. These spacings are created by lithiating CuOx particles, removing lithium oxides formed, and electrochemically reducing CuOx to metallic Cu. Also, the range of spacing (ds) is confirmed via the 3D tomographs using the Cs-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (3D tomo-STEM), and the operando X-ray absorption spectra show that oxidized Cu reduces to the metallic state during the CO2RR. Moreover, control of ds to 5–6 Å allows a current density exceeding that of unmodified CuOx nanoparticles by about 12 folds and a Faradaic efficiency of ≈80% to C2+. Density functional theory calculations support that ds of 5–6 Å maximizes the binding energies of CO2 reduction intermediates and promotes C–C coupling reactions. Consequently, this study suggests that control of ds can be used to realize the high activity and C2+ product selectivity for the CO2RR.

Copper (Cu) offers a means for producing value-added fuels through the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2), i.e., the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), but designing Cu catalysts with significant Faradaic efficiency to C2+ products remains as a great challenge. This work demonstrates that the high activity and selectivity of Cu to C2+ products can be achieved by atomicscale spacings between two facets of Cu particles. sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:

proposed that the electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is enhanced when hydrogen is confined between graphene and metal surfaces.[32] Furthermore, the second theoretical report examined the consequences of creating nanoscopic channels for the confined electrochemical oxygen evolution reaction (OER).[33] It proposed that the rate of the OER should be enhanced by having two surfaces located with a few angstroms of each other relative to that on flat surfaces.
In this work, we report that atomic-scale spacings between two facets of Cu nanoparticles enable high performance in the activity and product selectivity for the CO2RR. These spacings were created by subjecting CuOx nanoparticles to electrochemical lithiation followed by removal of lithium oxides deposited and electrochemical reduction of CuOx to Cu. Also, the 3D structures were elucidated by the 3D tomo-STEM method of individual CuOx nanoparticles and they exhibit that lithiation produces the desired interparticle spacing. Moreover, the operando X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra were used to investigate the in situ changes of the local atomic configurations of Cu nanoparticles during the CO2RR and we show that oxidized Cu reduces to the metallic state during CO2RR. Furthermore, Cu nanoparticles having the atomic-scale spacings of 5–6 Å are exhibited to give a high current density and an excellent FE to C2+ products, significantly higher than those reported for unmodified CuOx-derived Cu states.[8,17,24,34–36] Additionally, the DFT calculations of the binding energies for intermediates involved in CO2RR on Cu(100) and Cu(111) surfaces were employed to explore the CO2 reduction intermediates and C–C coupling mechanism involved in the CO2RR. When the spacing, ds, between such surfaces is 5–6 Å, we show that the binding energies for CO2 reduction intermediates (*COOH, *CO, *CHO, and *CHOH) reach maximum values and the formation of CC bonds via the reactions *CHO + *CO → *CHOCO and *CHO + *CHO → *CHOCHO is highly favored. Since *CHOCO and *CHOCHO are precursors to ethylene and ethanol,[15,37] the formation rates of C2+ products is expected to be maximized with ds = 5–6 Å. Therefore, these DFT calculations provide the atomistic details and molecularlevel understanding for an effect of the spacing between Cu planes on the CO2RR.

sections.heading: 2. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
2.1. Synthesis and Characterization of CuOx with Interparticle Spacings (ds)
The approach that we chose to create interparticle spacings is by electrochemical lithiation of CuOx nanoparticles. This process involves electrochemical reaction of Li+ cations with CuOx, which creates atomic-scale fractures in the particles.[38–40] CuOx nanoparticles having an average size of 50 nm were selected for lithiation. As shown in Figure 1a, the extent of lithiation was controlled by the cell potential used for each step. Discharge was carried out at 1.4, 1.2, 1, and 0 V, while charge was conducted at 3 V versus Li/Li+ using a static current of 10 mA g−1. The spacing between two facets of CuOx nanoparticles was controlled by halting the lithiation process at the designated point
in a charge/discharge profile. The lithiated particles were then washed with water before being characterized.
The evolution of the CuOx surface morphology during lithiation was illustrated in Figure 1b, and was confirmed by the ex situ TEM images (Figure 1c). Morphological evolution was observed for CuOx particles and fragments during lithiation (Figures S1–S4, Supporting Information). The lithiated nanoparticles exhibit rugged morphologies, as can be seen in the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (Figure S3, Supporting Information). The grain boundaries and defects in CuOx particles expand as lithiation progresses, ultimately developing into the interparticle spaces.
The atomic-scale defects and cracks in the CuOx particle at each step in the lithiation process were identified by the Cscorrected STEM analysis. An unmodified CuOx particle (blank), with an open smooth surface, is composed mainly of Cu2O, as detected by the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern (Figure S4, Supporting Information). Atomic-scale surface defects including grain boundaries were generated at step I (lithiation at 1.4 V), and the defect areas with the boundaries between different crystals were observed to be increased at step II (lithiation at 1.2 V). After steps I and II, the oxide phase was partially transformed to a reduced metallic phase (observable by the SAED pattern), and the surface was broken into polycrystalline fragments with abundant grain boundaries in the interspaces. At step III in the lithiation process (lithiation at 1.0 V), the combination of the atomic defects and their expansion resulted in angstrom-sized spaces between particles. As indicated by the STEM images (Figure 1d) of CuOx particles at step III, several angstroms-scale spacings between crystalline grains were detected in the reduced Cu phase. After lithiation (step IV, lithiation at 0 V), the partly reduced Cu fragments were separated and the interparticle distances of >1 nm were observed. Agglomerated particles were produced in the oxide phase following delithiation at step V (a recharge voltage of 3 V). The phase change of the CuOx particles occurring during lithiation was monitored by the powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses (Figures S5–S7, Supporting Information). These techniques show that the oxidation state of Cu is reduced during lithiation and increased after delithiation, which is consistent with information obtained from the SAED patterns (Figure S4, Supporting Information). It is notable that the Li2O and residual lithium in the lithiated samples were completely removed by washing after each lithiation step (see the experimental section for details), as confirmed by Li 1s XPS (Figure S7b, Supporting Information).
2.2. Probing Morphology of CuOx with Interparticle Spacings by the 3D Tomo-STEM Analysis
Additional information about the interparticle spacing and the morphology of the particle surfaces was obtained from analysis of the 3D model of a lithiated CuOx particle generated from the 3D tomo-STEM method. A 3D electron tomography is the technique to determine the precise structure of a sample in the atomic-scale resolution. Details of this method are described in Experimental Section and Figure S8 (Supporting Information).

Particular attention was given to the 3D electron tomographs of samples observed after steps III and IV in the lithiation process. A series of STEM images of CuOx particles after step III were obtained by rotating the sample holder (Figure 2a), then converting these images to projected images (Figure 2b), and finally creating the 3D structural model of the CuOx particle at step III (Figure 2c) through reconstruction of the projected images. Whereas the CuOx particle prior to lithiation (referred to as the blank) exhibited a smooth surface (Figure S9, Supporting Information), after step III in the lithiation process, atomic-scale spacings were created (Figure S10, Supporting Information). Figure 2d shows the distribution of ds observed in the 3D model for this sample. The value of ds lies between 3 and 18 Å, and the average value of ds is 6 Å. For the sample after step IV, relatively larger interparticle spacings were observed in the series of STEM images (Figure 2e) and the projected images (Figure 2f). The distribution of ds in CuOx after step IV was also collected using interparticle distances in the 3D model (Figure 2g and Figure S11, Supporting Information). After step IV in the lithiation process, the distribution of interparticle spacings observed in the reconstructed 3D model of CuOx (Figure 2h) is much broader, 3 Å to 30 Å, with an average value of ds = 15 Å. The large interplanar spacings observed after lithiation to step IV correspond to the formation of micropores (<20 Å).[41] Also, the size of the atomic-scale cracks in the CuOx particles was determined by analyzing the scale of interparticle spacing observed in TEM and STEM images (Figures S12–S14,

These results were compared to the spacing distribution obtained from the 3D model. The trends in the distribution of ds from TEM/STEM images are exhibited to be consistent with the information from the 3D tomographic projection model. Moreover, the pore size distribution determined from analysis of Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) isotherms is found to match well with the average spacing size determined after each lithiation step by the TEM analysis (Figure S15, Supporting Information). These support that the lithiation of CuOx nanoparticles leads to the formation of interparticle spacings ranging from 3.0 to 20 Å and that the average spacing of <10 Å is obtained at step III.
2.3. Electrochemical CO2RR of CuOx with Atomic-Scale Interparticle Spacings
The catalytic activity and product selectivity for CO2RR was evaluated by conducting ambient-pressure CO2 electrolysis in an H-type cell under a constant potential for several hours. To minimize the gradients in pH near the cathode, a 0.1 m CsHCO3 solution was used as the electrolyte and the cathode potential was kept above –1.0 V versus RHE.[29,31] We have shown previously that hydrated Cs+ cations can buffer pH changes occurring near the catalyst surface under conditions of considerable electrolyte polarization and, thereby, help to increase the amount of CO2 available for the CO2RR. More recently, it has been demonstrated that for cathode potentials more positive than −0.9 V versus RHE, hydrated Cs+ cations present in the outer Helmholtz layer impose a local electric field enhancing formation of CC bonds via coupling of adsorbed CO or adsorbed CO and HCO.[12,42] In addition, the evidence for the absence of mass transfer effects is identified from the Tafel analysis for the geometry-normalized current densities on lithiated CuOx samples (Figure S16, Supporting Information). Figure 3a reveals the geometric current densities of the unmodified and the lithiated samples as a function of the applied potential. At about −0.9 V versus RHE, the sample that had undergone lithiation up to step III exhibited a great increase in current density compared to that for the unmodified CuOx. It should be noted that the lithiated catalyst with an interplanar spacing also has a large electrochemical surface area (ESA) (Figure S17 and Table S1, Supporting Information), and the trend in the ESA is determined to be correlated with that for the BET surface area.
Figure 3b exhibits further the product distribution obtained from the unmodified and the lithiated samples at −0.9 V versus RHE. As ds increases, we find that the formation of C1 products gradually decreases, while the formation of C2+ products, particularly ethylene and ethanol (Figure 3b), increase significantly. It should be also noted that the H2 production is gradually suppressed by increasing ds. This effect is maximized at step III (ds < 1 nm), at which stage the C2H4/CH4 ratio rises to 54.3 and the FE for H2 decreases to 19%. Moreover, the onset potential for C2H4 formation decreases to −0.5 V versus RHE, which is ≈300 mV lower than the potential for the unmodified
sample (Figure S18, Supporting Information). After lithiation to step IV having the random distribution of ds > 10 Å, the selectivity to C1 products and hydrogen recovers, and the FE for C2H4 falls to a level observed after step V. The FE as a function of the overall applied potential is presented in Figure S19a (Supporting Information). It shows that repeated lithiation cycles (5, 10, and 20 cycles) result in a CO2RR activity similar to that achieved after step V (Figure S19b, Supporting Information). In addition, we note that the surface roughness changes during lithiation steps. The geometrically normalized product current densities (Figure S20, Supporting Information) match with the trend for product current densities (Figure S21, Supporting Information) normalized by the specific surface area (SSA), indicating that the surface roughness could contribute to the formation of C2+ products. However, we observe a mismatch between the surface roughness and the catalytic activity from samples III and IV. Sample IV with ds > 1 nm showed the highest surface roughness of 23.04 (EDLCIV/EDLCBlank, Table S1, Supporting Information), but its current density and product selectivity toward C2+ products were inferior to those of sample III (ds < 1 nm) having a surface roughness of 20.15 (EDLCIII/EDLCBlank, Table S1, Supporting Information). Moreover the partial current densities for C2+ products and FEs of the major CO2RR products obtained at −0.9 V versus RHE are illustrated as a function of the lithiation step in Figure 3c,d. The highest current density for C2+ products is observed for a certain range of ds (<1 nm, step III), which is ≈12-fold higher than that seen for the unmodified sample. On the other hand, those for H2 and C1 products, including CO, formate, and CH4, are reduced. The high current density is ascribed to both the increased electrochemically active surface area and also the decrease in the free energy barrier for the reduction of CO2.
Since the catalyst activity and selectivity have been reported to depend on the catalyst mass loading,[35] we explored further the effect of catalyst mass loading on the selectivity to C2+ products using CuOx with ds < 1 nm. Catalysts were prepared by drop-casting 50 to 150 µL of the catalyst-containing solution onto the glassy carbon substrate. The measured activities and FEs for C2+ products are shown in Figure 3e and Figure S22 (Supporting Information). We find that the performance of CuOx with ds < 1 nm and an optimal mass loading (100 µL, equivalent to 11.4 µg cm−2 of Cu) exhibits the maximum FE for C2+ products in nearly 80% and a 1 h average FE of ≈75%. These results support that the C2+ FE achieved by creating ds of 5–6 Å significantly exceeds those for Cu nanoparticles prepared by other techniques.[17,23,35]
All catalyst samples were characterized after CO2RR in order to determine whether other parameters besides, ds, could contribute to the enhanced activity and selectivity of Cu for the CO2RR, e.g., electrochemically induced changes in nanoparticle morphology, the presence of oxidized Cu, grain boundaries at the surface of Cu nanoparticles, and nanoparticle roughness. The ex situ TEM images (Figure S23a, Supporting Information) show that none of the samples exhibited a significant change in morphology after CO2RR. Likewise, the magnitude of ds remained relatively constant after CO2RR. The stability of ds is also reflected in the stability of the current density observed for several hours under the applied potential (Figure S23b, Supporting Information). Since the importance of Cu oxidation

state and subsurface O on the activity and selectivity of Cu for the CO2RR has been noted in previous studies,[17,21–23] we evaluated the oxidation state of our catalysts after their use for the CO2RR. The XRD peaks show that CuOx was immediately reduced to metallic Cu[43] upon applying a potential of −0.9 V versus RHE (Figure S24a, Supporting Information), suggesting that CO2RR occurs on metallic Cu. This finding was also confirmed by the operando XAS spectra acquired for an applied potential of −0.9 V versus RHE. The XANES and EXAFS spectra of the blank sample and samples with ds demonstrate that after CO2 reduction at −0.9 V versus RHE all samples are reduced to the metallic copper regardless of the initial oxidation state of Cu (Figure S24b, Supporting Information). The results show that oxidized Cu species, e.g., Cu+, are completely reduced during the CO2RR. Recent studies conducted using 18O-labeled H2O, together with theoretical studies of the stability of subsurface O, also support that subsurface O is extremely unstable in Cu and will be rapidly removed upon application of reducing potentials well below those used for the CO2RR.[42,44] Both of studies also support the conclusion that Cu can be rapidly reoxidized by the very small amount of O2 dissolved in H2O when the metal is not held under a reducing potential. Therefore, the cumulative evidence suggests that none of oxidation states of Cu or subsurface O is a significant contributor to the changes in the CO2RR activity and selectivity observed upon lithiation of Cu nanoparticles. A number of recent studies have found that with the increasing surface roughness the FE for C2+ products increases, whereas the FEs for H2 and CH4 decrease. These trends are ascribed to an increase in the fraction of undercoordinated sites

Theoretical studies confirm that undercoordinated sites bind CO more strongly than more fully coordinated sites on planar surfaces, thereby increasing the surface coverage of CO and decreasing the coverage of adsorbed H.[7,45] Studies of a simulated rough Cu surface also show that OCCHO, a precursor to C2 products, binds more strongly, particularly on Cu(100)-like square sites next to a Cu(111)-like step surface and on-top of a twin boundary that binds *OCCOH parallel to the twin boundary.[45] The authors then project that the FE to C2 products should increase with the density of grain boundaries.
Given the enhanced roughness of the inter-particle surfaces of CuOx produced by lithiation (Table S1, Supporting Information), we can propose the surface roughness as one of contributors to the enhanced activity and C2+ selectivity, as well as the suppression of CH4 formation observed as a consequence of CuOx lithiation at step IV and V. Meanwhile, Figure 3d supports that the sample prepared at step III exhibits the highest FE to C2+ products (nearly 80%) and the lowest FE to CH4 (3%) of any of the lithiated samples examined, which emphasizes again that the controlled atomic-scale spacing of ds < 1 nm outperforms the effect by the surface roughness. The electric field at small pores has been also suggested as one of factors for the enhanced CC coupling.[30,31] However, the electrical double-layer overlapping in the sub-nanometer scale gap weakens the electric field effect, which is inconsistent with the boosted catalytic activity at ds of 5–6 Å. Therefore, this leads to a conclusion that the atomic gap is the key activity descriptor for the enhanced CO2RR.
An important question then is whether the density of GBs could be the primary factor responsible for this product distribution. To this end, we compared the surface density of GBs determined from an analysis of TEM images, as described in Section S7 and Figure S25a (Supporting Information). We note that the GB surface density increased after steps I and II of the lithiation process, but then decreased sharply at step III (Figure S25b, Supporting Information). This observation suggests that while the density of GBs may be a contributor to the enhanced partial current density and FE for C2+ products at steps I and II in the lithiation process, it is not the dominant factor defining the product distribution at step III. Since the optimal activity and selectivity of lithiated CuOx occurs for interparticle spacings of <1 nm (Figure 3d and Figure S26, Supporting Information). This suggests that the presence of Cu planes with such atomic distances between them contributes significantly to the overall performance of Cu nanoparticles, even if the fraction of Cu surfaces with such spacing may be relatively low.

sections.heading: 2.4. DFT Calculations of the Binding Energies for CO2 Reduction Intermediates As Well As CC Coupling Reactions Involved in the CO2RR
sections.text:
Based on these findings, we conducted DFT calculations of the binding energies for various species hypothesized to be involved in both the CO2RR with the aim of identifying the effects of atomic-scale spacing between Cu surfaces on the rate and selectivity of the CO2RR. Copper nanoparticles with different atomic-scale spaces between them were simulated using a model consisting of two three-layer Cu (100) and Cu (111)
(3 × 3) slabs, where the surfaces are separated by the distance ds (Figure 4a). It should be noted that increasing the number of layers from three to five leads to insignificant changes in the energetics. These calculations were carried out assuming a vacuum above the Cu surfaces and the effect of the electrode potential was taken into account using the hydrogen potential electrode method.[46]
The binding energies (BEs) for *COOH, *CO, *CHO, *CHOH, and *H, adsorbed species thought to be involved in the CO2RR[9,10,47] and the HER,[48] were determined as a function of ds. As illustrated in Figure 4b, the BEs of *COOH, *CO, *CHO, and *CHOH strongly depend on ds, whereas the opposite is true for *H. For example, the variation of the BE for *COOH is 0.52 and 0.44 eV for Cu(100) and Cu(111), respectively, whereas it is only 0.01 eV for *H. Importantly, the strongest BEs for *COOH, *CO, *CHO, and *CHOH occur for values of ds between 5.2 Å and 5.8 Å. The changes in BE relative to that for Cu (100) and Cu(111) are −0.52 and −0.44 eV for *COOH, −0.09 and −0.07 eV for *CO, −0.24 and −0.21 eV for *CHO, and −0.18 and −0.17 eV for *CHOH (Figure 4b and Table S2, Supporting Information), whereas it is nearly zero for *H. These results suggest that for *COOH, *CHO, and *CHOH, in particular, there is a thermodynamic driving force for the migration of these species from open Cu(100) and Cu(111) surfaces toward the spaces between nanoparticles with the optimal value of ds. Calculations of the free energy for the reaction sequence of * + CO2(g) + (H+ + e−) → *COOH + (H+ + e−) → *CO + H2O(l) + (H+ + e−) → *CHO carried out for an applied bias of U = −0.9 V versus RHE reveal that this sequence of reactions is energetically favored when the spacing between Cu surfaces is ds = 5.2 Å, rather than 9 Å (Figure 4c). We also calculated the BE of *COH and find that it is larger than that of *CHO at all the ds values considered in this work, suggesting the reduction of CO2 proceeds through *CHO rather than *COH.
We examined next whether the value of ds affects the energetics of CC bond formation. The coordinates of the optimized structures used to construct the potential energy surfaces have been fully determined. Since *CO and *CHO are the early stage intermediates for CO2RR and therefore their concentrations are expected to be higher than the others, the changes of the reaction energies for CC coupling of *CHO + *CO → *CHOCO were evaluated. We found that the reaction energies depend strongly on ds and that the minimum values relative to open Cu(100) and Cu(111) surfaces occur at ds = 5.0 and 6.0 Å, respectively (Figure 4d). It is notable that the minimum reaction energies are more favorable than those for Cu(100) by −0.95 eV and Cu(111) by −0.48 eV, which suggests that Cu surfaces separated by the optimal value of ds will promote the C−C coupling reaction of *CHO + *CO → *CHOCO. The ds also has profound effect on formation of C−C bonds via the reaction *CO + *CO → *OCCO. For Cu(111), when ds ≤ 5.6 Å, stable *OCCO is formed, and importantly as ds decreases, the reaction energy decreases from 1.24 eV for ds = 5.6 Å to 0.43 eV for ds = 4.6 Å. Similarly, for Cu(100), when ds ≤ 5.6 Å, stable *OCCO is formed, and as ds decreases, the reaction energy decreases from 0.91 eV for ds = 5.6 Å to −0.36 eV for ds = 4.2 Å. These results suggest that Cu surfaces separated by the optimal 5–6 Å should promote CC coupling via the reactions *CHO + *CO → *CHOCO and *CO + *CO → *OCCO.

Calculations of the free energy for the reaction sequence of *CHO + *CO + (H+ + e−) → *CHOCO + (H+ + e−) → *CHOCHO were carried out for an applied bias of −0.9 V versus RHE. Our calculations (Figure 4e) show that the first step (CC coupling) is downhill by −0.43 eV for Cu (100) and −0.19 eV for Cu(111) when ds = 5.2 Å, whereas it is uphill by +0.42 eV for Cu (100) and uphill by +0.30 eV for Cu (111) when ds = 9 Å (or +0.50 eV for Cu (100) and +0.33 eV for Cu (111)). Since this step does not involve an electron transfer, its energetics are not affected by the applied bias. This finding suggests that the Cu facets with an optimal value of ds = 5–6 Å should facilitate CC bond formation, which is energetically unfavorable on open Cu(100) and Cu(111) surfaces.
To understand why atomic-scale spacing between the Cu(100) and Cu(111) surfaces helps stabilize adsorbed species, we carried out a Bader analysis of the charge transfer from the two surfaces. These calculations show that the enhancement
in adsorption strength for adsorbed species is due to charge transfer from the second layer to the adsorbate. For example, for *CO, the second layer donates 0.15 electron to the adsorbate compared to 0.38 electron from the first layer, and for *CHOCO, the second layer donates 0.65 electron to the adsorbate, which is similar to the amount donated by the first layer (0.60 electron), and optimal stabilization occurs when ds = 5 to 6 Å. This finding is consistent with our experimental results, where enhanced activity toward C2+ products was maximized at the samples with ds < 1 nm.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we demonstrated that atomic-scale spacings between two facets of Cu nanoparticles enhance the activity of Cu and its selectivity to C2+ products including ethylene

and ethanol. It was proven that lithiating CuOx nanoparticles and then removing the lithium oxides deposited lead to creation of atomic-scale spacings. The sizes of these spacings could be controlled by the extent of lithiation and the range of the spacing was confirmed by the 3D tomo-STEM method for individual CuOx particles. Also, the operando XANES and EXAFS spectra demonstrated that as-synthesized spacings are retained even upon reduction of the oxide particles to metallic copper. Moreover, the experimental investigations exhibited that control of the atomic-scale interlayer spacing between two facets of Cu nanoparticles allows to achieve high activity and C2+ product selectivity, and low CH4 selectivity for the CO2RR. When the spacings between the facets of metallic Cu reached atomic dimensions, in particular 5–6 Å, an order of magnitude increase in the current density was observed for the CO2RR for a given applied potential and the product selectivity to ethylene and ethanol rises to nearly 80%, which is higher than that attainable for Cu nanoparticles produced by reduction of thermally or plasma oxidized Cu. Furthermore, when parallel Cu(100) and Cu(111) surfaces spaced ≈5–6 Å apart, the DFT calculations revealed that the binding energies of species involved in the formation of CC bonds are increased and the energetics for the formation of such bonds become more favorable. Consequently, our combined study of experimental and theoretical investigations supports that control of ds could pave a new route to enhance the activity of Cu for the CO2RR and the product selectivity to ethylene and ethanol.

sections.heading: 4.1. Experimental Method: Materials
sections.text: Copper oxide nanoparticles (99.5+%) were purchased from EPRUI Nanoparticles & Microspheres Co. Ltd. The lithium foil (99.999%) and the copper foil (99.9999%) were purchased from Honjo Chemical Corp. and UACJ Foil Corp., respectively. The electrolyte for the lithiation process was purchased from Sigma Aldrich and the electrolyte for CO2 reduction reaction was prepared with the deionized (DI) water. All reagents unless otherwise stated were obtained from commercial sources (Sigma Aldrich and Merck) and were used without purification.

sections.heading: 4.2. Experimental Method: Preparation of Copper Oxide Nanoparticles with Controlled Interparticle Spaces
sections.text:
CuOx (EPRUI Nanoparticles & Microspheres Co. Ltd.) was cleaned by annealing under argon at 150 °C for 3 h before the experiments. The lithiated CuOx nanoparticles were prepared using the following procedures described in our previous work.[39] At first, CuOx nanoparticles were mixed with 5 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) dispersed in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP). Next, the black slurry was uniformly coated onto a Cu foil and dried overnight in a vacuum oven at 80 °C. A coin-type cell with the Li foil as the counter electrode and 1 m LiPF6 dissolved in a mixture of ethyl carbonate (EC) and diethyl carbonate (DEC) as the electrolyte (1/1 = v/v) were used for the electrochemical lithiation. The cells containing the Li foil
and working electrodes were assembled with a separator (Celgard) and an electrolyte in an Ar-filled glove box (O2 < 0.1 ppm and H2O < 0.1 ppm). The lithiation process was monitored using a VSP potentiostat (Bio-logic) to maintain the static current of 10 mA g−1. After the lithiation process was carried out, the resulting samples produced at each process step were washed with acetone, water, and 1 × 10−3 m acetic acid solution to remove residual electrolytes, Li2O, and solid electrolyte interlayers.

sections.heading: 4.3. Experimental Method: 3D Tomo-STEM Method
sections.text: The 3D tomo-STEM analysis was conducted using the Titan (T4) at the KAIST analysis center for research advancement (KARA). The electron scanning projections were obtained by 120° rotating from −55° to 65°. A tunable electron-beam acceleration of 200 keV was utilized. A 120-times analysis was performed to obtain the projected images for each one-degree of angle rotation. The axis of rotation was aligned, and 2D projections were reconstructed using the “inspect 3D” software of Thermo Fisher and generate 880 cross-sectional images. The reconstructed file was transferred to the “Avizo” algorithm and processed for the boundary on every cross-sectional image. Then, the particle segmentation to recognize the substances separated from each particle was made on the projected images using the interactive threshold. After segmentation, the finite element method was applied to construct the 3D model structure of a CuOx nanoparticle from the 3D volumes obtained through the integration of surfaces. To measure the distance of atomic-scale spacing, the label-analysis has been performed on the distances between particles in the 3D-structure, based on a finite element model. The method for image processing in this work has been also reported previously.[49]

sections.heading: 4.4. Experimental Method: Material Characterization
sections.text:
The ex situ scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscope images were obtained using a JSM-7600F (JEOL) SEM and a JEM-ARM200F (JEOL) TEM, respectively. The powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data were collected using a SmartLab θ–2θ diffractometer operated in the reflectance Bragg-Brentano geometry with a Johansson type Ge (111) monochromator filtering the Cu Kα1 radiation at a power of 1200W (40 kV, 30 mA). The diffractometer was equipped with a high speed 1D detector (D/teX Ultra). Moreover, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra were obtained through a Thermo VG Scientific Sigma Probe instrument using a 350 W Al anode X-ray source with a multianode, a pulse counter, and a hemispherical analyzer. The spectra were collected using an incident photon energy of 1486.6 eV and corrected by using the detector work function. Additionally, the ex situ and in situ (operando) synchrotron X-ray measurements were carried out at Pohang Accelerator Laboratory (PAL, Republic of Korea), being operated at the 3.0 GeV energy with a maximum storage current of 300 mA. X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) analyses including the X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and the extended X-ray absorption fine

sections.heading: 4.5. Experimental Method: Characterization of the Electrochemical CO2RR
sections.text:
Lithiated Cu2O nanoparticles were spin coated onto a glassy carbon substrate, which was then used as the cathode for electroreduction of CO2 in a 0.1 m CsHCO3 solution. The reason for using Cs+ cations is described elsewhere.[29] The electrolyte was first sparged with CO2 to attain a pH of 6.8. Electrochemical measurements were conducted using a Biologic SP-300 potentiostat. CO2 electrolysis was performed in a custom-made electrochemical cell,[50] in which the working electrode is parallel to the counter electrode and the geometric area for both of the electrodes was 1 cm2. The average mass loading of samples on working electrode is 80 µL (equal to ≈10 µg cm−2), which was measured using an ultramicrobalance (XP2U d = 0.1 µg, Mettler Toledo). In order to optimize the catalytic activity, mass loading of catalyst solutions was controlled from 50 to 150 µL. In order the separate the anodic and cathodic chambers (1.3 mL each), a Selemion AMV anion-exchange membrane (110 µm thick) was used. The electrolyte of the cathodic compartment was saturated with CO2 for at least 15 min prior to conducting electrolysis. CO2 was sparged during the electrolysis at a flow rate of 5 sccm. The counter electrode was a platinum foil and the reference electrode was an Ag/AgCl electrode (leak free series) from Innovative Instruments, Inc. All collected data were rescaled to the RHE using the following equation of

The solution and charge transfer resistances were measured using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy by scanning from 1 MHz to 10 Hz prior to the electrolysis and all reported CVs and electrolysis, measurements were made IR-compensated.

sections.heading: 4.6. Experimental Method: Product Analysis
sections.text:
Gaseous products were analyzed with a gas chromatograph (SRI instruments) equipped with a packed HaySep D column and a packed MolSieve 5 A column. CO, CH4, C2H4, and C2H6 were detected using a flame ionization detector (FID) with a methanizer in He as the carrier gas. H2 was analyzed using a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) in a nitrogen carrier gas. Calibration of the gas chromatograph was performed using a calibration gas obtained from Praxair (UN 1956). On-line gas product analysis was carried out every 25 min by flowing CO2 directly into the gas-sampling loop of the gas chromatograph during 1.5 h electrolysis. Faradic efficiencies were obtained by averaging the individual product analysis. Soluble products were collected from the cathodic and anodic
compartments after electrolysis and subsequently analyzed in the high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using an Ultimate 3000 instrument from Thermo Scientific. The column of an Aminex HPX 87-H column (Bio-Rad) was used with diluted sulfuric acid (1 × 10−3 m) as an eluent. The temperature of the column oven was maintained at 60 °C and the separated soluble products were analyzed by a refractive index detector (RID).

sections.heading: 4.7. Theoretical Method: Density Functional Theory Calculation
sections.text:
All the DFT calculations using the slab models were performed using the dispersion-corrected PBE-D2 functional[51,52] and the projector augmented wave pseudopotentials[53,54] with a 400 eV cut-off basis set, as implemented in the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP).[55–58] To accelerate the convergence for energies using self-consistent field (SCF) iterations, the Gaussian-smearing technique (smearing temperatures kBT = 0.1 eV for slabs and 0.01 eV for molecules) was employed, after which all calculated energy values were extrapolated to kBT = 0. The reciprocal space for the slab was sampled by a Monkhorst-Pack k-point net of 3 × 3 × 1, whereas only the gamma point was sampled for the molecular calculations. The models were prepared from a face-centered cubic copper bulk structure with a lattice parameter of 3.615 Å. To prevent interactions between the periodic replicas along the z-direction, a vacuum separation of at least 15 Å between adjacent images was used for the slab calculations and a 20 Å × 20 Å × 20 Å box was used for the molecular calculations. Spin-polarized wave functions were also used for all the surface calculations, whereas spinrestricted wave functions were used for H2, H2O, and CO2. During the geometry optimization, the copper atoms in the top layer of the upper surface and those in the bottom layer of the lower surface were fixed. Although in the initial structure the distance of d between the two surfaces is set to be a target value, it would be slightly different from the value by less than 0.2 Å after optimization, depending on the identity of the adsorbate. The energetics reported here are based on electronic energies. For example, the binding energy of *COOH is given by BE (*COOH) = E (*COOH) − E (*) − E (CO2) − 0.5 × E (H2). Therefore, a more negative value of BE denotes the stronger adsorption.
